title: Home energy audits and assessments in Ontario (2026): cost, rebates, deadlines and energy advisors
h1: Home energy audits and assessments in Ontario: the 2026 guide
description: How a home energy assessment works in Ontario in 2026: what the EnerGuide evaluation measures, what it costs, how to find a registered energy advisor, the $600 Home Renovation Savings rebate and its December 31 deadline, and whether a free audit exists.
blurb: The whole Ontario picture: what a home energy assessment measures, what it costs, how to find an energy advisor, the $600 rebate and its 2026 deadline, and the free option.
lede: In Ontario, a home energy audit means an EnerGuide home energy assessment: a registered energy advisor measures your house, rates it, and hands you a ranked list of upgrades. It's also the ticket to the province's biggest renovation rebates, and in 2026 who does it and when matter more than they used to.

sections.h2: What an Ontario home energy assessment actually is
sections.html:
An energy audit, a home energy assessment and an EnerGuide evaluation are the same service in Ontario. A registered energy advisor working for a service organization licensed by Natural Resources Canada assesses the house from basement to attic: the insulation in walls, ceilings and basement, the windows and doors, the heating, cooling, hot-water and ventilation equipment, and a blower door test that measures air leakage. The data goes into energy modelling software, and you get an EnerGuide rating and a report on possible upgrades (NRCan ↗). The first visit takes about two hours, the follow-up about one (Home Renovation Savings ↗).

Ontario's rebate programs work on two visits: an initial assessment before you renovate and a follow-up assessment afterwards that measures what changed. Anything you do before the first visit doesn't count.

sections.h2: What a home energy assessment costs
sections.html:
Few advisors publish prices, so expect to ask. Typical Ontario prices are about $500–$700 for the initial assessment and $200–$450 for the follow-up, plus HST where it applies. Windfall Ecology Centre charges $500 and $250 plus HST (Windfall ↗); Reep Green Solutions charges $540 and $406 with no HST, as a registered charity (Reep ↗); and the City-backed programs in London and Waterloo Region tell participants to expect $500–$700 for the first visit (BetterHomes London ↗, RetrofitWR ↗). NRCan puts the two visits together at $600–$1,000 on average (NRCan ↗). Bigger homes cost more. Our Ontario cost guide lists the providers who publish their rates.

The Home Renovation Savings rebate covers up to $600 of that bill, but only if both assessments come from one of the seven approved organizations below and you finish the program's steps in time. Windfall and Reep aren't among the seven.

Ontario's Home Renovation Savings program, run by Enbridge Gas and Save on Energy, pays up to $600 toward your two assessments once you've completed at least two recommended upgrades. On top of that: insulation up to $7,700, $100 per window or door opening, $200–$250 for air sealing, $500 for a heat pump water heater, and a $500 bonus for three or more upgrades (program page ↗). Totals are capped at $5,000 per home if you heat with Enbridge gas, or $10,000 if you heat with electricity, oil, propane or wood, the $600 included.

The deadline is what matters now. The follow-up assessment has to be booked by November 30, 2026 and completed within 180 days of the first visit or by December 31, 2026, whichever comes first, and rebates are paid only while program funding lasts (program terms ↗). Starting this fall means booking the initial assessment now and lining up contractors before the report arrives.

Gas-heated homes qualify only as Enbridge Gas customers. If your gas comes from Kitchener Utilities or Utilities Kingston, confirm eligibility with the program before you book.

sections.h2: Finding an energy advisor in Ontario
sections.html:
Energy advisors don't work alone: each is registered with NRCan and works through a licensed service organization, which is who you book with (NRCan ↗). NRCan lists the licensed organizations for existing homes by province (NRCan ↗), and our Ontario directory lists them by region with review links.

Any registered advisor can give you an official EnerGuide rating. For the Home Renovation Savings rebates, though, the assessments must come from one of the program's seven approved service organizations: AmeriSpec, Canada Energy Audit, Greenbrain, Energuy, Energy Werx, NRGwise and The Home Inspectors Group (program FAQ ↗). The program emails you that list after you fill in its eligibility form.

Every other licensed organization, the community non-profits included, is still the right call for everything else: financing such as Toronto's HELP loans, heat pump sizing, a pre-purchase rating, or simply knowing where your heating money goes. Our guide to energy audit companies in Ontario lists every licensed option.

sections.h2: Is there a free home energy audit in Ontario?
sections.html:
Not for most households. The free route is income-tested: Save on Energy's Energy Affordability Program sends an energy-efficiency expert for a free energy needs assessment and, in homes heated by electricity or oil, can add insulation, draft proofing, a programmable or smart thermostat and a cold-climate heat pump at no cost. It covers households under its income limits (from $48,220 for one person to $127,576 for seven or more) and people receiving benefits such as ODSP, Ontario Works, LEAP, OESP or the Guaranteed Income Supplement (Save on Energy ↗).

A "free audit" from an insulation, window or HVAC company is a sales visit, not an EnerGuide assessment, and it won't qualify you for any rebate.

For a house, an energy audit is never legally required to sell or renovate in Ontario. It's required by the programs that pay you: the Home Renovation Savings assessment path and most Toronto HELP loans. Large buildings are different: owners of buildings of 50,000 sq ft and up must report energy and water use every year (ontario.ca ↗). Details in when an energy audit is required in Ontario.

1. Decide whether you want the Home Renovation Savings rebates. If you do, use one of the seven approved organizations and move before the fall deadlines.
  2. Get two or three quotes. Ask for the price of both visits and the current wait for a first appointment.
  3. Book the initial assessment, and don't start any work before it.
  4. Complete at least two of the recommended upgrades with contractors of your choice.
  5. Book the follow-up assessment with the same organization, then submit your invoices for the rebates.

Not sure what your house needs yet? The Home Energy Planner reads your home's era and symptoms and lists the tests to ask for by name.

faq.q: How much does a home energy assessment cost in Ontario?
faq.a: Typical Ontario prices are about $500–$700 for the initial EnerGuide assessment and $200–$450 for the follow-up, plus HST where it applies; NRCan puts the two together at $600–$1,000 on average. Home Renovation Savings pays back up to $600 once you complete at least two upgrades, but only for assessments from its seven approved organizations, with the follow-up done within 180 days or by December 31, 2026, whichever comes first.

faq.q: Are there free home energy audits in Ontario?
faq.a: Only for income-qualified households. Save on Energy's Energy Affordability Program includes a free energy needs assessment and, in homes heated by electricity or oil, free insulation, draft proofing, thermostats and a cold-climate heat pump, for households under its income limits or receiving benefits such as ODSP or Ontario Works. For everyone else, the $600 Home Renovation Savings rebate recovers most of the cost of two assessments from an approved organization.

faq.q: How do I find a registered energy advisor in Ontario?
faq.a: Book through a service organization licensed by NRCan: NRCan's list of service organizations for existing homes covers Ontario, and our directory lists them by region. If you want the Home Renovation Savings rebates, choose one of its seven approved organizations: AmeriSpec, Canada Energy Audit, Greenbrain, Energuy, Energy Werx, NRGwise or The Home Inspectors Group.

faq.q: What is the deadline for the Ontario energy audit rebate?
faq.a: The follow-up assessment must be booked by November 30, 2026 and completed within 180 days of the initial assessment or by December 31, 2026, whichever comes first, and rebates are paid only while funding lasts.

faq.q: Is an energy audit the same as an energy assessment?
faq.a: Yes. In Ontario an energy audit, a home energy assessment and an EnerGuide evaluation are the same service, delivered by an NRCan-registered energy advisor.

blurb: Province by province: $500–$700 plus a follow-up in Ontario with $600 back through approved organizations, $150 + tax in Quebec, $99 + HST in NB and PEI, $400 back in Manitoba — and what drives the price.
lede: A home energy audit — an EnerGuide evaluation in Canada — usually costs a few hundred dollars, and in several provinces a program pays most or all of it. Here's what you'll actually pay in 2026, province by province, and what moves the price.

sections.html: Where the market sets the price, expect about $500–$700 for a first EnerGuide evaluation in Ontario, plus $200–$450 for a follow-up visit if a rebate program needs one, plus HST where it applies. • Size and complexity. Larger homes take longer to model: Windfall adds $50–$150 above 2,500 sq ft, and Reep $50–$275 above 3,000 sq ft.
  • One visit or two. Rebate programs usually need a follow-up assessment after the work, billed separately.
  • Distance. Rural and northern addresses can carry travel fees.

  • Who sets the fee. In Quebec and PEI the program sets it; elsewhere the service organization does.

The fee buys two things. First, the report: an airtightness number and a room-by-room model that stop expensive mistakes, such as an oversized heat pump or new windows in a house whose real problem is the attic. Second, access: in Ontario the assessment path unlocks up to $5,000 in rebates for gas-heated homes and $10,000 for homes heated by electricity, oil, propane or wood, and in BC the Improvement Bonus pays on the measured change between two evaluations.

sections.h2: Commercial building audits cost more — and have their own funding
sections.html: Offices, apartment buildings and plants get engineering audits to the ASHRAE Standard 211 levels, priced by floor area and the depth of analysis. In Ontario, Enbridge Gas pays up to 50% of pre-approved audits and engineering studies for customers using 100,000 m³ of gas a year or more, capped at $10,000 per project ($20,000 for institutions) (Enbridge ↗). More in our guide to commercial and industrial energy audits.

A free visit from a company that sells insulation, windows or heating equipment isn't an EnerGuide evaluation. There's no blower door, no rating and no rebate eligibility, and the recommendations tend to match what the company sells. Real free assessments exist, but they come through income-qualified programs, not sales teams.

Home Renovation Savings pays back up to $600 after two or more upgrades, but only for assessments from its seven approved organizations, with the follow-up done within 180 days or by December 31, 2026, whichever comes first.

faq.q: How much does an EnerGuide evaluation cost in Quebec?
faq.a: $150 plus tax through Rénoclimat, with the evaluator assigned by the program rather than chosen by you. The $150 is reimbursed when you receive Rénoclimat assistance (the tax isn't), and the first post-retrofit evaluation is free, so participants who do the work pay about $22.46.

faq.q: Why do energy audit prices vary so much?
faq.a: Home size, the number of visits, travel distance and add-ons such as an F280 heat-loss calculation all change the price — and in some provinces a program sets the fee instead of the market.

title: Commercial and industrial energy audits in Ontario (2026): ASHRAE levels, costs and incentives
h1: Commercial and industrial energy audits in Toronto and Ontario
description: Energy audits for Ontario commercial, institutional and industrial buildings: ASHRAE Level 1–3 explained, who performs them, reporting rules (50,000 sq ft provincially, 10,000 sq ft in Toronto from 2027), Enbridge's 50% audit incentive and Save on Energy's programs.
blurb: ASHRAE Levels 1–3 explained, who performs them, Toronto's reporting rules, Enbridge's 50% audit incentive and Save on Energy's building programs.
lede: Houses get an EnerGuide evaluation. Offices, apartment towers, schools, plants and warehouses get an engineering energy audit: scoped to a recognized standard, priced by size, and in Ontario often half-funded by the gas utility. Here's how it works and who does it.

sections.html:
Commercial energy audits in North America are scoped to ASHRAE Standard 211, the standard for commercial building energy audits (ANSI/ASHRAE/ACCA 211 ↗). It defines three levels, each building on the last:

  • Level 1 — walk-through. A site visit and a review of utility bills that benchmark the building and list low-cost and no-cost measures, plus candidate projects worth studying.
  • Level 2 — energy survey and analysis. A detailed breakdown of where the energy goes, with savings and cost estimates for each measure. Most capital plans and incentive applications are built on this level.
  • Level 3 — detailed analysis of capital-intensive projects. Monitoring, modelling and engineering-grade estimates for the big-ticket decisions, sometimes called investment-grade.

Ask any firm you're considering which level its quote covers and which sections of the ASHRAE 211 report it will deliver. "Energy audit" on its own can mean anything from a two-hour walk-through to months of metering.

Building audits are engineering work, delivered by mechanical engineering firms and energy consultancies. Look for licensed engineers (P.Eng., licensed by Professional Engineers Ontario) signing the recommendations, and credentials such as the Certified Energy Manager (CEM). For condo and apartment buildings, building-science firms often lead, because the envelope matters as much as the plant.

Energy management services are the ongoing half: utility monitoring and benchmarking, retro-commissioning, and strategic energy management programs that keep savings from drifting away after the audit. Save on Energy funds several of these directly (below).

The residential EnerGuide system is separate. Its service organizations and registered energy advisors are licensed for houses and low-rise homes, not commercial buildings.

sections.h2: The reporting rules in Toronto and Ontario
sections.html:
• Ontario (EWRB): buildings of 50,000 sq ft and larger report energy and water use to the province every year by July 1 (ontario.ca ↗).
  • City of Toronto: buildings of 50,000 sq ft and larger have reported to the City since 2024, due July 2 each year, using ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager. Buildings of 10,000 sq ft and larger join in 2027, after the City postponed the expansion in December 2025 (toronto.ca ↗).
  • Toronto's Building Emissions Performance Standards are still being designed. Council approved the approach in July 2024; limits, thresholds and dates haven't been set, and low-rise residential buildings of three storeys or fewer are exempt (toronto.ca ↗).

Reporting isn't auditing, but it produces the benchmark that tells an owner whether an audit will find much. A building that scores poorly against its peers is the one to audit first.

sections.h2: Who pays: Ontario incentives for audits and upgrades
sections.html:
Enbridge Gas pays up to 50% of eligible assessment costs — energy audits, engineering feasibility studies, steam trap surveys, air and water balancing, and metering — capped at $10,000 per project for commercial customers and $20,000 for institutions. You need to be an Enbridge customer using at least 100,000 m³ of gas a year, and the study must be pre-approved before it starts (Enbridge commercial audits ↗). Industrial customers have a parallel stream for process and steam studies, also at up to 50%, with work completed between January 1 and November 30 (Enbridge industrial studies ↗).

Save on Energy (the IESO) funds the electricity side: the Retrofit Program for equipment and controls, Existing Building Commissioning, the pay-for-performance Energy Performance Program, the Expanded Energy Management Program, XLerate for large industrial, municipal, institutional and healthcare projects, Peak Performance for summer peak reductions, and Instant Discounts (Save on Energy ↗).

Level 1 walk-throughs are the cheapest; Level 2 and Level 3 work scales with floor area, the number of systems and how much metering and modelling is involved. Ask for a fixed fee per level and a list of deliverables, and ask whether the firm will prepare the Enbridge pre-approval. On a qualifying project the utility can cover half the fee.

If you own a house, a duplex or a small low-rise, you need an EnerGuide assessment instead — see energy audit services in Toronto and our Toronto directory. Toronto's HELP loans cover low-rise buildings of up to 3 storeys and 6 units.

faq.q: What is the difference between an ASHRAE Level 1, 2 and 3 energy audit?
faq.a: Level 1 is a walk-through with a utility-bill review and a list of low-cost measures. Level 2 breaks down where the energy goes and prices each measure. Level 3 adds monitoring and detailed modelling for capital-intensive projects.

faq.q: Does Enbridge pay for commercial energy audits?
faq.a: Yes. Enbridge Gas pays up to 50% of eligible audits and engineering studies, capped at $10,000 per project for commercial customers and $20,000 for institutions. You need at least 100,000 m³ a year of gas use and pre-approval before the study starts.

faq.q: Do Toronto buildings have to report energy use?
faq.a: Buildings of 50,000 sq ft and larger report energy and water use to the City every year, due July 2. Buildings of 10,000 sq ft and larger start reporting in 2027.

faq.q: Who can perform a commercial energy audit in Ontario?
faq.a: Mechanical engineering firms and energy consultancies, ideally with licensed engineers (P.Eng.) and Certified Energy Managers on the project. The residential EnerGuide licence doesn't cover commercial buildings.

title: Energy audits for multi-unit residential buildings (MURBs) in Canada: who rates them and which programs pay
h1: Energy audits for duplexes, triplexes and apartment buildings
description: How energy audits work for multi-unit residential buildings (MURBs) in Canada: EnerGuide ratings for low-rise buildings and the separate NRCan exam advisors need, engineering audits for larger buildings, and the Ontario and federal programs that do and don't cover them.
blurb: EnerGuide for low-rise MURBs and the advisors qualified to rate them, engineering audits for larger buildings, and which programs cover multi-unit homes.
lede: A duplex, a six-plex and a 1960s apartment tower all count as multi-unit buildings, but they get different audits. Low-rise buildings can get an EnerGuide rating from an energy advisor who has passed NRCan's separate MURB exam; larger buildings get an engineering energy audit. Which one you need also decides which programs will pay.

sections.html:
NRCan's EnerGuide Rating System covers low-rise multi-unit residential buildings (MURBs). When the federal Greener Homes Grant funded them, NRCan defined an eligible MURB as one with three or fewer storeys above ground, a building area of 600 m² or less, 2 to 100 units stacked or joined by a common space, and at least half its floor area used as living space. It also required one evaluation of the whole building, every unit and common area included, rather than unit-by-unit ratings (NRCan ↗).

High-rise buildings are a different job: NRCan says they involve very different engineering and fall outside the EnerGuide Rating System. Mid- and high-rise apartment buildings and condos get an engineering energy audit scoped to ASHRAE Standard 211, from a mechanical engineering firm or a certified energy manager. Our guide to commercial and multi-residential audits explains the three ASHRAE levels.

Not every energy advisor can. Advisors register with NRCan for houses first, then can add EnerGuide for MURBs by passing a separate, optional MURB exam. NRCan requires it for anyone who evaluates MURBs, issues a MURB label or submits MURB files (NRCan ↗). When you call a service organization about a duplex, triplex or small apartment building, ask whether the advisor they'd send is registered for MURBs.

Tell us it's a multi-unit building when you ask to be matched, and we'll only introduce you to an advisor who confirms MURB registration.

sections.h2: Federal options for owners and landlords
sections.html:
• CMHC Eco Improvement refunds 25% of your CMHC mortgage insurance premium after $20,000 of energy upgrades. It covers owner-occupied loans on 1–4 units and small rental loans on 2–4 units (our guide).
  • CMHC MLI Select gives owners of rental buildings with 5 or more units points toward better mortgage-insurance terms when they commit to cutting an existing building's energy use and emissions: a 15% cut earns 20 points, 25% earns 35, and 40% earns 50. The energy analysis has to come from a professional engineer, architect, certified engineering technologist or certified energy manager, using energy simulation software (CMHC ↗).

1. Count storeys and units. Three storeys or fewer, with a building area of 600 m² or less, points to an EnerGuide MURB evaluation. Anything larger points to an engineering audit.
  2. Ask about MURB registration before you book an EnerGuide evaluation.
  3. Match the audit to the money. Hi-RIS asks for an ASHRAE Level 2 report or better, MLI Select for an energy analysis by an engineer, architect, technologist or energy manager, and the city loan programs for EnerGuide evaluations before and after.

faq.q: Can a duplex or triplex get an EnerGuide rating?
faq.a: Yes, as a multi-unit residential building, if the advisor is registered for EnerGuide for MURBs, which takes a separate NRCan exam. Low-rise buildings within NRCan's MURB limits qualify: three storeys or fewer above ground and a building area of 600 m² or less. High-rises fall outside the EnerGuide Rating System.

faq.q: Does Ontario's Home Renovation Savings program cover multi-unit buildings?
faq.a: Its assessment path doesn't: duplexes, triplexes, stacked townhouses and multi-unit buildings are excluded. In Toronto, Ottawa and Peterborough, the city loan programs do cover small multi-unit buildings.

faq.q: What audit does a Toronto apartment building need for Hi-RIS?
faq.a: An energy assessment report at ASHRAE Level 2 or above; the City may accept a decarbonization study for non-profit housing. Hi-RIS is for Toronto apartment buildings at least 20 years old with 7 or more units and 3 or more storeys.

faq.q: Who can do the energy analysis for CMHC MLI Select?
faq.a: A professional engineer, architect, certified engineering technologist or certified energy manager, using energy simulation software. For existing buildings, cuts of 15%, 25% or 40% earn 20, 35 or 50 points.

title: Heat pump rebates in Toronto and Ontario (2026): what you can actually get
h1: Heat pump rebates in Toronto and Ontario
description: Toronto has no City heat pump rebate in 2026. What you can get: Home Renovation Savings pays up to $7,500 for a cold-climate heat pump ($12,000 ground-source, $2,000 in Enbridge gas-heated homes), HELP finances the rest, and income-qualified homes heated by electricity or oil can get one free. Checked October 8, 2026.
blurb: No City rebate in 2026, but up to $7,500 provincially ($2,000 if gas-heated), HELP financing, city top-ups elsewhere in Ontario, and free heat pumps for income-qualified homes.
lede: There's no City of Toronto heat pump rebate in 2026: the City's HELP incentives, heat pumps included, ran from July 2022 to January 2025 and are fully subscribed. What Toronto homeowners can get is the provincial rebate, City financing and, for income-qualified households, a heat pump installed free. Here's the stack, checked on October 8, 2026.

sections.h2: The provincial rebate: Home Renovation Savings
sections.html:
Across Ontario, heat pump rebates come from the no-assessment stream of Home Renovation Savings. The amount depends on how you heat today and on the kind of heat pump (program page ↗):

How you heat nowCold-climate air-sourceGround-source
Electricity, oil, propane or wood$1,250 per ton, up to $7,500$2,000 per ton, up to $12,000
Enbridge natural gas$500 per ton, up to $2,000$3,000
Renting the heat pump (any fuel)$500 per ton, up to $2,000$3,000

Worked through: a 3-ton cold-climate heat pump replacing electric baseboards earns 3 × $1,250 = $3,750; the same unit in a gas-heated home earns 3 × $500 = $1,500, and the furnace can stay as backup.

The rules that trip people up:

  • Use a participating contractor, and wait for written pre-approval before buying. Anything installed before approval gets nothing.
  • Replacing an existing heat pump doesn't qualify, and new homes must have been occupied for at least six months.

title: Vermiculite insulation in Canadian homes: when it was used, how to spot it, and testing
h1: Vermiculite insulation: when it was used, how to spot it, and what to do
description: Most vermiculite attic insulation came from the Libby, Montana mine, worked from the 1920s to 1990 and sold mainly as Zonolite — often contaminated with asbestos. How to recognize it, why you shouldn't disturb it, how testing works, and what it means for an insulation upgrade.
blurb: Mined at Libby, Montana from the 1920s to 1990 and sold mostly as Zonolite: how to recognize it, how testing works, and what it means before any attic upgrade.
lede: If your attic is filled with loose, pebbly granules — grey-brown or silvery-gold — instead of fluffy batts or blown fibre, you may have vermiculite insulation. Most of it is harmless left alone, but it changes how any insulation or air-sealing work has to proceed.

sections.html:
Health Canada traces the problem to one source: vermiculite ore from the Libby mine in Montana, worked from the 1920s to 1990, which supplied most of the world's vermiculite insulation, mostly under the brand name Zonolite. It wasn't widely used after the mid-1980s and hadn't been sold in Canada for more than a decade when Health Canada issued its advisory in 2004 (Health Canada ↗).

So the homes to check are those built or re-insulated before about 1990 — and "re-insulated" matters, because vermiculite was often poured into older attics as a top-up decades after the house was built.

Vermiculite insulation looks like light, pebble-sized granules that pour like gravel between the attic joists. The flakes are flat and shiny, silver-gold to grey-brown (CCOHS ↗). It can also turn up inside wall cavities. Look from the attic hatch with a flashlight; don't reach in and handle it.

Not all vermiculite contains asbestos, but vermiculite insulation sold in Canada before 1990 may, because much of the Libby ore was contaminated with amphibole asbestos (CCOHS ↗). Inhaled asbestos fibres can cause asbestosis, mesothelioma and lung cancer, and the illnesses are usually tied to frequent, prolonged exposure (Health Canada ↗).

The reassuring part: Health Canada says there's currently no evidence of a health risk while the insulation stays sealed behind walls and floors or isolated in the attic. The danger comes from disturbing it — renovating, running wires or ducts through the attic, air sealing from above, or storing things up there.

Testing tells you what you have, and it's a job for a professional: CCOHS advises having a competent person test before any renovation. A qualified sampler wets the material, collects bulk samples and sends them to an accredited lab; expect roughly $50–$150 per sample. Because contamination varied from batch to batch, results depend on proper sampling, which is why a DIY kit isn't the answer. Our asbestos and vermiculite testing guide walks through the process.

sections.h2: What it means for an energy upgrade
sections.html:
An attic full of vermiculite is usually exactly the attic that needs air sealing and more insulation — and both jobs disturb it. So the order matters:

  1. Flag it before the energy assessment, so the advisor notes it and doesn't disturb it.
  2. Have it sampled before any contractor quotes attic work.
  3. If it tests positive, choose between managing it in place (no attic work, sealed hatch, no storage) and professional removal before insulating.
  4. Only then book the air sealing and insulation — and remember that Ontario's Home Renovation Savings attic work has to be installed by November 30, 2026 (no-assessment stream) or finished before a December 31, 2026 follow-up (assessment path).

• Leave it alone. Don't vacuum it, move it or store boxes on it.
  • Seal the gaps — cracks and openings where it could sift into the living space, and the attic hatch (CCOHS ↗).
  • Test before any renovation that touches the attic, walls or ceilings below it.
  • Hire a qualified removal contractor if it has to come out. Never remove suspected asbestos-containing vermiculite yourself.

faq.q: When was vermiculite insulation used in Canada?
faq.a: Most came from the Libby, Montana mine, worked from the 1920s to 1990 and sold mainly as Zonolite. It wasn't widely used after the mid-1980s, so homes built or re-insulated before about 1990 are the ones to check.

faq.q: Does all vermiculite insulation contain asbestos?
faq.a: No. But vermiculite insulation sold in Canada before 1990 may contain asbestos, because much of it came from the contaminated Libby mine. Only lab testing of properly collected samples tells you what you have.

faq.q: Is vermiculite dangerous if I leave it alone?
faq.a: Health Canada says there is currently no evidence of a health risk while it stays sealed behind walls and floors or isolated in the attic. The risk comes from disturbing it.

faq.q: Can I add insulation on top of vermiculite?
faq.a: Not without dealing with it first. Adding insulation and air sealing both disturb it, so have it tested, then either leave the attic alone or have it professionally removed before the work.

faq.q: How much does vermiculite testing cost?
faq.a: Roughly $50–$150 per lab sample when a qualified professional collects bulk samples and sends them to an accredited lab.

title: Home energy testing in BC: FAQ on EnerGuide evaluations, F280 heat-loss calculations, blower doors and radon
h1: Home energy testing in BC: your questions answered
description: Answers for BC homeowners: what an EnerGuide evaluation includes, when a CSA F280 heat-loss calculation is required (including Okanagan heat pump sizing), what blower door numbers mean, radon testing, and how the Home Energy Improvement Bonus pays $750–$2,000.
blurb: EnerGuide evaluations, the F280 calculation BC heat pump rebates require, blower door numbers, radon, and the $750–$2,000 Improvement Bonus.
lede: BC's programs lean on measurement more than most provinces': the Home Energy Improvement Bonus pays on the measured change between two EnerGuide evaluations, and heat pump rebates require a CSA F280 heat-load calculation. Here are the questions BC homeowners ask most.

sections.h2: What does a home energy evaluation include in BC?
sections.html: An EnerGuide home evaluation by an NRCan-registered energy advisor: a blower door test for air leakage, an inventory of insulation, windows, doors and heating and hot-water equipment, and a computer model of the house. You get an EnerGuide rating in gigajoules per year and a renovation upgrade report (NRCan ↗). Better Homes BC keeps a list of program-qualified energy advisors ↗.

sections.h2: Do I need an evaluation for BC rebates?
sections.html: For the Home Energy Improvement Bonus, yes. It pays $20 for every percentage point your EnerGuide rating improves, from $750 to $2,000, once you install at least three bonus-eligible upgrades. It needs a pre-upgrade and a post-upgrade evaluation by a program-qualified advisor, with the upgrades and the post-upgrade evaluation done within 18 months of the first, and you apply within six months of the post-upgrade evaluation. Doing only two upgrades? The separate $300 Two Upgrade Bonus needs no evaluation: install two bonus-eligible upgrades within 18 months of each other and apply within six months of the second invoice. It's one bonus per property (Better Homes BC ↗). The per-measure rebates from BC Hydro and FortisBC have their own requirements; see our Improvement Bonus page.

sections.h2: What is a CSA F280 calculation, and when do I need one?
sections.html:
CSA F280 is the Canadian standard for working out how much heating and cooling capacity a house needs, room by room, at its local design temperature. BC's rebate rules make it mandatory in the most common case: for an air-source heat pump replacing electric heat, the contractor must complete a heat-load calculation using CSA F280-12 verified software at the home's design temperature, and northern dual-fuel heat pumps need a program-approved calculation (Better Homes BC ↗).

Expect about $150–$400 as a standalone service, or less when bundled with an evaluation (our F280 guide).

sections.h2: Why F280 sizing matters in the Okanagan
sections.html: Kelowna, Vernon and Penticton have milder winters than the north but hot, dry summers, so a heat pump there does double duty. F280 covers both heating and cooling loads, and a proper calculation stops the two classic mistakes: a unit sized to the old furnace, which is often too big, and one sized for winter alone, which can struggle on 35°C afternoons. Ask the contractor for the F280 report by name and check it uses your home's actual design temperatures.

sections.h2: What do blower door numbers mean?
sections.html: The main result is ACH50: how many times per hour the house's whole air volume leaks out and gets replaced at a test pressure of 50 pascals. Lower is tighter. The advisor also estimates the leakage area and, with a smoke pencil or thermal camera, shows you where the leaks are. After air sealing, the follow-up test measures what you gained — the number the Improvement Bonus pays on. More in our blower door guide.

sections.h2: Should I test for radon in BC?
sections.html: Yes. Health Canada recommends every home test, with a long-term test of at least three months in the heating season; the Canadian guideline is 200 Bq/m³ (Health Canada ↗). Radon varies house by house, so a neighbour's result doesn't tell you yours. Test before air sealing and again afterwards. Our radon guide covers kits and mitigation.

sections.h2: Are there free options in BC?
sections.html: For income-qualified households, yes. The CleanBC Energy Savings Program installs upgrades at no cost, and BC Hydro's Energy Conservation Assistance Program has income limits from $51,100 for one person to $135,100 for seven or more (BC Hydro ↗). BC also delivers the federal Greener Homes Affordability Program.

faq.q: Do BC heat pump rebates require an F280 heat loss calculation?
faq.a: Yes, for air-source heat pumps replacing electric heat: the contractor must complete a heat-load calculation using CSA F280-12 verified software at the home's design temperature. Northern dual-fuel heat pumps need a program-approved calculation.

faq.q: How much does an F280 calculation cost?
faq.a: Roughly $150–$400 as a standalone service, or less when bundled with an EnerGuide evaluation.

faq.q: How does the BC Home Energy Improvement Bonus work?
faq.a: It pays $20 per percentage point of EnerGuide improvement, from $750 to $2,000, after three bonus-eligible upgrades, with pre- and post-upgrade evaluations by a program-qualified advisor. The upgrades and the post-upgrade evaluation must be done within 18 months of the first evaluation, and you apply within six months of the second. With only two upgrades, the $300 Two Upgrade Bonus applies instead, with no evaluation needed.

faq.q: What is a good blower door result?
faq.a: Lower ACH50 is better. The number matters most as a before-and-after comparison: the follow-up test shows what your air sealing achieved.

faq.q: Should I test for radon before air sealing?
faq.a: Yes. Health Canada recommends a long-term test of at least three months; test before tightening the house and again afterwards. The guideline is 200 Bq/m³.

title: Home energy audits in Oakridge, London ON: what 1950s–1970s homes need, rebates and local advisors
h1: Home energy audits in Oakridge, London
description: What a home energy audit finds in Oakridge's 1950s–1970s homes, the tests to ask for, the Ontario rebates that fit (with the December 31, 2026 deadline), and the registered advisors serving London.
blurb: 1950s–1970s homes: what audits find in Oakridge, the tests to ask for, the rebates that fit, and who serves London.
lede: Oakridge grew in London's post-war expansion, and its ranches and bungalows share a predictable energy story: thin original insulation, basements that were never meant to be living space, and furnaces reaching the end of their life. An EnerGuide assessment turns that story into numbers — and into rebates.

sections.h2: What Oakridge homes are made of
sections.html: Most of Oakridge was built from the 1950s to the 1970s: single-storey ranches and bungalows. Original batts were thin by today's standards, attics often started around R-10, and basements were left bare. Many owners are now finishing those basements — the moment an audit pays off most, before the drywall goes up.

sections.h2: What an audit usually finds here
sections.html:
• Attics far below today's target. Topping up toward R-50 is typically the fastest payback in the house.
  • Rim joists and top plates leaking air. The blower door shows these clearly; sealing them is cheap.
  • Uninsulated basement walls in homes where the lower level is becoming living space.
  • Aging mid-efficiency furnaces facing the furnace, hybrid or heat pump decision.
  • Aluminum wiring in some later builds — worth flagging before any insulation work.

• The blower door test (standard in every EnerGuide assessment) with a thermal camera walk-through.
  • An attic inspection that checks for vermiculite — common in attics insulated before 1990 — before anyone disturbs it.
  • A combustion safety check if you still have a naturally vented water heater or older furnace and plan to air-seal.
  • A heat-loss calculation before replacing the furnace — small bungalows are often sold oversized equipment.

Oakridge is textbook territory for Ontario's Home Renovation Savings assessment path: attic insulation (up to $1,500), air sealing ($200–$250) and basement insulation (up to $2,300) are two- and three-upgrade combinations that unlock the $600 assessment rebate, and three or more add a $500 bonus. Gas-heated homes are capped at $5,000 in total. Book the assessments through one of the program's seven approved service organizations, and have the follow-up done by December 31, 2026 — the program is only funded through 2026.

h1: Heat pump rebates in Canada by province (2026)
description: Every province's heat pump rebate in 2026, checked on official pages October 8, 2026: Ontario up to $7,500 ($12,000 ground-source), Quebec's LogisVert, B.C.'s $4,000 and income-tiered CleanBC rebates, Manitoba, Atlantic Canada and the North, plus which federal programs closed and when.
blurb: Province-by-province heat pump rebates for 2026 with amounts, conditions and official links, the federal programs that closed and when, and where we found nothing.
lede: There's no national heat pump rebate in 2026: the federal Greener Homes Grant stopped taking applications in 2024 and the Oil to Heat Pump Affordability Program on July 31, 2026. What's left is provincial and utility money, and it ranges from up to $13,000 for some lower-income B.C. households to nothing we could find in Alberta and Saskatchewan. Here's every province and territory, checked on October 8, 2026.

sections.h2: Federal heat pump money: what closed and when
sections.html:
• Canada Greener Homes Grant: applications ran from May 2021 to February 2024, and December 31, 2025 was the last day to upload documents (NRCan ↗). More on the closed grant.
  • Canada Greener Homes Loan: October 1, 2025 was the last day to apply; loans already approved continue (CMHC ↗).
  • Oil to Heat Pump Affordability Program: July 31, 2026 was the last day to apply. Approved participants have until January 31, 2027 to upload final receipts, and the program closes March 31, 2027 (NRCan ↗). Our OHPA page.
  • Canada Greener Homes Affordability Program: free heat pumps and insulation for low-to-median-income households, delivered only through partners in BC, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, PEI and Quebec (NRCan ↗); Hydro-Québec's registration for 2026–27 has ended (Hydro-Québec ↗).
  • CMHC Eco Improvement: if you bought with a CMHC-insured mortgage, a heat pump counts toward the $20,000 of energy work that earns a 25% refund of your mortgage insurance premium (our guide).

sections.h2: Ontario: up to $7,500, or $12,000 for ground-source
sections.html:
Ontario's heat pump rebates come from the no-assessment stream of Home Renovation Savings, run by Enbridge Gas and Save on Energy. The amount depends on how you heat today (program page ↗):

  • Electricity, oil, propane or wood: cold-climate air-source $1,250 per ton, up to $7,500; ground-source $2,000 per ton, up to $12,000.
  • Enbridge Gas customers heating with natural gas: $500 per ton, up to $2,000, or $3,000 for ground-source. The furnace can stay as backup.
  • Rented heat pumps, any fuel: $500 per ton, up to $2,000, or $3,000 for ground-source.

A participating contractor files for pre-approval, and nothing installed before written approval qualifies. Replacing an existing heat pump doesn't count, and oil-heated homes must size the new electric heating to replace the oil heat completely (program FAQ ↗). The heat pump page lists no installation deadline or end date.

If your gas comes from Kitchener Utilities or Utilities Kingston rather than Enbridge, check eligibility before you plan around the gas-home amounts: the program is written for Enbridge Gas customers or for homes heated by electricity, oil, propane or wood (program terms ↗).

Free for income-qualified homes: Save on Energy's Energy Affordability Program installs a cold-climate heat pump at no cost in eligible homes heated by electricity or oil, for households under its income limits ($48,220 for one person up to $127,576 for seven or more) or receiving benefits such as Ontario Works, ODSP, OESP or LEAP (Save on Energy ↗).

City programs add money in some places:

  • Waterloo Region (GrandBridge Energy customers): RetrofitWR loans at 2.5% with up to $2,500 toward eligible heat pumps, plus $1,000–$3,000 for income-eligible households (RetrofitWR ↗).
  • Ottawa: Better Homes Ottawa loan participants get $700 per ton for a cold-climate air-source heat pump or $1,000 per ton for ground-source (Better Homes Ottawa ↗); the City says new loan applications are currently waitlisted.
  • Guelph: loans are closed, but low-income households can get grants of up to $15,000 for an air-source heat pump (City of Guelph ↗).
  • London: BetterHomes London loans at 2.5% come with income-based incentives of up to $10,000 (BetterHomes London ↗).

More detail for the Toronto area is in heat pump rebates in Toronto and Ontario.

The City of Toronto doesn't offer a heat pump rebate in 2026. Its Home Energy Loan Program (HELP) lends up to $125,000, or 10% of your home's assessed value if less, repaid on your property tax bill, and projects that include a heat pump qualify for a 20-year term. A heat-pump-only project doesn't need EnerGuide assessments; the installer signs an attestation instead (toronto.ca ↗).

The City did pay HELP incentives, heat pumps included, from July 7, 2022 to January 24, 2025, and that funding is fully subscribed (HELP terms ↗). In Toronto, the rebate itself comes from Home Renovation Savings. See our HELP guide for rates and steps.

sections.h2: Quebec: LogisVert and the dual-energy offer
sections.html:
Hydro-Québec's LogisVert pays $50 per 1,000 BTU/h of capacity at −8°C for an ENERGY STAR certified heat pump, or $120 for a model classified cold-climate, and its page puts the maximum at $6,700. Heat pumps installed on or after November 26, 2025 must be ENERGY STAR certified. In eligible multi-unit buildings, installs from June 15, 2026 can get a bonus of $100 more per 1,000 BTU/h. New geothermal systems get $750 per 1,000 BTU/h, deducted on the installer's invoice, up to $54,000 for a house (Hydro-Québec ↗).

Homes heated with natural gas have a separate offer. Under the Chauffez vert dual-energy offer, Énergir customers can get $7,300 and Enbridge Gaz Québec customers $6,800 to add an electric central heat pump to a forced-air gas system, with gas kept as the backup for the coldest days and Hydro-Québec's Rate DT applying to the electricity (Hydro-Québec ↗).

Rénoclimat doesn't pay for heat pumps; since October 1, 2026 it pays for insulation, high-performance windows, backup power and flood protection.

sections.h2: British Columbia: rebates by heating fuel and income
sections.html:
B.C.'s Home Renovation Rebate program, funded by BC Hydro and FortisBC with the Province, pays $4,000 for a heat pump that meets 100% of the home's heating at −5°C, or $1,500 for one that meets at least half, but only when it replaces electric heating. Rebates for switching from oil (up to $6,000) or gas and propane (up to $8,000) apply only north of and including the District of 100 Mile House (Better Homes BC ↗). For an air-source heat pump completed, invoiced and paid between August 1 and October 31, 2026, BC Hydro adds up to $1,000 while funding lasts (BC Hydro ↗).

Lower- and middle-income households can use the CleanBC Energy Savings Program: up to $13,000 toward a central heat pump replacing oil, gas or propane at Level 1, $7,000 at Level 2 and $3,500 at Level 3, deducted on a registered contractor's invoice (Better Homes BC ↗). FortisBC electricity customers with electric heat can borrow up to $6,500 at 1.9% over 10 years instead of taking a rebate (FortisBC ↗).

Better Homes BC's page of municipal top-ups now returns "page not found" (Better Homes BC ↗), so we don't list any B.C. city top-ups as current.

Manitoba has the Prairies' only provincial heat pump rebates: $2,000 for a centrally ducted cold-climate air-source heat pump and $1,500 for a ductless one, supplementing electric or gas heat (propane and oil conversions also qualify) (Efficiency Manitoba ↗). Ground-source systems can go in with no upfront cost and an interest-free $75 monthly payment for 15 years on the Manitoba Hydro bill (Efficiency Manitoba ↗), and income-qualifying households can get a heat pump free (Efficiency Manitoba ↗).

In Saskatchewan we found none: SaskPower and SaskEnergy list no residential heat pump rebate, and the Home Efficiency Retrofit Rebate ended in April 2026 (SaskPower ↗). Saskatoon's Home Energy Loan Program finances heat pumps. Details in Saskatchewan rebates and the tax credit.

Alberta has no provincial rebate either. Clean Energy Improvement Program loans can finance a heat pump in 27 municipalities, with an EnerGuide evaluation required (CEIP ↗), but Calgary's intake is closed until winter 2026/27 and Edmonton's is waitlisted. See energy efficiency rebates in Alberta.

• New Brunswick: through Total Home Energy Savings, a central ducted heat pump earns $1,500, a heat pump added to a furnace $1,000, geothermal $2,000, a mini-split $400 and a multizone system $350 per indoor head, after a $99 + HST evaluation (SaveEnergyNB ↗). Oil-to-heat-pump advance payments closed to new registrations on June 30, 2026 (SaveEnergyNB ↗).
  • Nova Scotia: Home Energy Assessment rebates pay $300 per ton for ductless, $500 per ton for centrally ducted and $600 per ton for closed-loop geothermal heat pumps; the Moderate Income Rebate adds $500 or $1,500 per ton for homes not heated mainly by electricity (rebate guide ↗). Efficiency Nova Scotia stopped taking federal oil-to-heat-pump applications on July 2, 2026 (Efficiency Nova Scotia ↗).
  • Prince Edward Island: "On April 15, 2026, heat pump rebates ended," and free heat pump applications are closed (PEI ↗). Heat pumps bought between April 15, 2025 and April 15, 2026 can still be claimed within a year of purchase.
  • Newfoundland and Labrador: the takeCHARGE Oil to Electric program is still accepting applications: up to $9,000 for a central heat pump replacing oil or propane, $6,500 for multi-splits and $5,000 for an electric furnace or boiler, or $22,000, $18,000 and $10,000 if income-qualified (takeCHARGE ↗). The new income-eligible TakeCharge Greener Homes Program offers a limited number of no-cost heat pumps for projects completed after October 5, 2026 (takeCHARGE ↗).

sections.h2: Yukon, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut
sections.html:
Yukon pays 50% of the cost of a heat pump in an existing home, up to $10,500, or 100% up to $24,000 through the income-qualified Affordable Heat Pump Program, which needs approval before you install. Homes must keep their existing heating as backup (Government of Yukon ↗).

The Northwest Territories' Arctic Energy Alliance lists no heat pump rebate and no longer funds heating systems that use fossil fuels (AEA ↗). In Nunavut we found no heat pump program, and Nunavut homes were never eligible for the federal oil-to-heat-pump program because of grid requirements (NRCan ↗). More in territorial energy programs.

1. Size it first. A CSA F280 heat-loss calculation sizes the heat pump to the house, not to the old furnace, and air sealing or insulation done first can shrink the unit you need.
  2. Get approval before you buy wherever the program asks for it: Ontario's rebate and Yukon's income-qualified program pay nothing for equipment installed before approval.
  3. Check the installer is registered with the program: participating contractors in Ontario, the Home Performance Contractor Network in B.C., registered contractors in Manitoba, RBQ licences in Quebec.
  4. Estimate running costs before you compare quotes with our energy cost calculator, and read switching to a heat pump.
  5. Keep every invoice and the equipment's model number; programs ask for them when you claim.

faq.q: When do heat pump rebates end?
faq.a: It depends on the program. The federal Oil to Heat Pump Affordability Program closed to new applications on July 31, 2026, PEI's heat pump rebates ended on April 15, 2026, and BC Hydro's limited-time bonus covers installs paid by October 31, 2026. Ontario's Home Renovation Savings heat pump page, Quebec's LogisVert, Efficiency Manitoba and Newfoundland and Labrador's Oil to Electric program listed no end date when we checked on October 8, 2026.

faq.q: What is the Ontario heat pump rebate in 2026?
faq.a: Through Home Renovation Savings: $1,250 per ton, up to $7,500, for a cold-climate air-source heat pump, or $2,000 per ton, up to $12,000, for ground-source, in homes heated by electricity, oil, propane or wood. Enbridge gas-heated homes get up to $2,000 (air-source) or $3,000 (ground-source). You need a participating contractor and written pre-approval, but no energy assessment.

faq.q: Does the City of Toronto have a heat pump rebate?
faq.a: No. The City offers HELP loans of up to $125,000 (or 10% of assessed value), repaid on your property tax bill; its HELP incentives, which included heat pumps, ran from July 2022 to January 2025 and are fully subscribed. The rebate in Toronto comes from the provincial Home Renovation Savings program.

faq.q: Is there a federal heat pump rebate in 2026?
faq.a: Not for most households. The Greener Homes Grant and the Oil to Heat Pump Affordability Program are closed. Low-to-median-income households in BC, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, PEI and Quebec can get free upgrades through the Greener Homes Affordability Program's provincial partners, and CMHC Eco Improvement refunds 25% of a CMHC mortgage insurance premium after $20,000 of energy work, a heat pump included.

faq.q: Can I get a heat pump rebate if I heat with natural gas?
faq.a: In some provinces. Ontario pays Enbridge Gas customers up to $2,000 (air-source) or $3,000 (ground-source); Quebec's dual-energy offer pays $7,300 or $6,800 to add a central heat pump to a gas furnace; Manitoba's air-source rebates cover heat pumps supplementing gas heat. In B.C., gas-to-heat-pump rebates outside the income-qualified program apply only north of 100 Mile House.

faq.q: Do I need an energy audit to get a heat pump rebate?
faq.a: Not in Ontario, Quebec, B.C. or Manitoba for the heat pump rebate itself. In New Brunswick and Nova Scotia the rebates come through the home energy evaluation, so you need one first. Everywhere, a heat-loss calculation is how the system should be sized.

title: Energy efficiency rebates in Alberta (2026): what exists, what doesn't, and CEIP financing
description: What Alberta homeowners can get in 2026: no provincial rebate, Clean Energy Improvement Program financing in 27 municipalities (Calgary closed until winter, Edmonton waitlisted), Lethbridge's $1,350 CEIP rebate, Medicine Hat's HAT Smart evaluation rebates, and the federal options that still apply. Checked October 8, 2026.
blurb: No provincial rebate in 2026, CEIP financing in 27 municipalities with Calgary closed and Edmonton waitlisted, Medicine Hat's HAT Smart rebates, and the federal options that remain.
lede: Alberta has no provincial home energy-efficiency rebate in 2026, and the federal grants that used to fill the gap are closed. The main help left is Clean Energy Improvement Program (CEIP) financing, repaid on your property tax bill, and most of the large-city intakes are full or closed this fall. Lethbridge and Medicine Hat add small rebates of their own. Here's what exists, as of October 8, 2026.

sections.h2: What the province offers: nothing we could find
sections.html:
We found no provincial home energy-efficiency rebate in Alberta as of October 8, 2026. The Government of Alberta's energy-efficiency programs page, which used to list provincial help, now returns "page not found" (alberta.ca ↗). The City of Edmonton's program page says, "Currently, there are no available rebates" for residents (City of Edmonton ↗).

The federal money that used to fill the gap is also gone. The Oil to Heat Pump Affordability Program, which NRCan delivered directly in Alberta, closed to new applications on July 31, 2026 (NRCan ↗), and the Greener Homes Affordability Program has no Alberta delivery partner (NRCan ↗).

The Clean Energy Improvement Program (CEIP) is financing, not a rebate. Your municipality pays for approved upgrades, and you repay through a charge on your property tax bill, over up to 20 years for some upgrades, and can pay the balance off at any time. Alberta Municipalities delivers it with the participating municipalities, and an EnerGuide Home Energy Evaluation is required as part of the process (CEIP ↗).

It covers detached and semi-detached homes, townhouses and low-rise apartment buildings in 27 municipalities: Airdrie, Banff, Beaumont, Calgary, Canmore, Cold Lake, Devon, Drayton Valley, Edmonton, Grande Prairie, Jasper, Lac La Biche County, Leduc, Lethbridge, Medicine Hat, Okotoks, Pincher Creek Region, Rocky Mountain House, Spruce Grove, St. Albert, Stettler, Stirling, Strathcona County, Sturgeon County, Taber, Westlock and Wetaskiwin (CEIP locations ↗). Each sets its own rate, cap and intake.

sections.html:
Here's where the larger programs stood this fall:

sections.h2: Municipal rebates: Medicine Hat's HAT Smart
sections.html:
Medicine Hat runs its own rebate program, HAT Smart, for customers of the City's electric, natural gas and water utilities. It pays up to $250 toward a pre-renovation EnerGuide evaluation and up to $250 toward the post-renovation one, as a credit on your utility account, for evaluations completed from January 1 to December 15, 2026. The advisor must hold a City of Medicine Hat business licence and put the HAT Smart or CEIP program code on the receipt, and the rebate closes once its funds are paid out (City of Medicine Hat ↗).

HAT Smart's Existing Homes incentive, which covers insulation, windows and doors, tankless water heaters, heat and energy recovery ventilators and solar panels up to $5,000 per home, has been fully subscribed since September 29, 2026 and isn't taking new requests (City of Medicine Hat ↗). Other municipalities may run programs of their own, so check your city's website before you book.

We found no heat pump rebate in Alberta, and Medicine Hat's HAT Smart list doesn't include them. CEIP can finance air-source heat pumps along with high-efficiency furnaces and boilers, but rules differ: in Edmonton a gas furnace qualifies only when it's installed with a heat pump (CEIP ↗).

Without a rebate, sizing is the whole game. A CSA F280 heat-loss calculation keeps the heat pump matched to the house, and our energy cost calculator compares running costs with your current furnace. For other provinces' rebates, see heat pump rebates in Canada by province.

There's no provincial rebate for insulation, windows or air sealing either, and Medicine Hat's HAT Smart incentive for them is fully subscribed for 2026. CEIP can finance them in participating municipalities, and the EnerGuide evaluation it requires ranks them for your house. Outside CEIP, the return comes through your heating bills, which is why an energy audit still earns its keep: a blower door test shows where the air is leaking before you spend on the fix.

• CMHC Eco Improvement: bought with a CMHC-insured mortgage? Complete at least $20,000 of qualifying energy renovations and CMHC refunds 25% of your mortgage insurance premium; apply within 2 years of closing (CMHC ↗). Our guide.
  • Canada Greener Homes Grant: closed; applications ran from May 2021 to February 2024 (NRCan ↗).
  • Canada Greener Homes Loan: closed; October 1, 2025 was the last day to apply (CMHC ↗).

1. Check whether your municipality is on the CEIP list and whether its intake is open.
  2. If you plan to finance through CEIP, pre-qualify first, then book the EnerGuide evaluation; in Edmonton, upgrades already started or completed can't be financed.
  3. In Medicine Hat, book the evaluation with an advisor who holds a City business licence and puts the HAT Smart or CEIP code on the receipt, so you can claim up to $250 back for each evaluation.
  4. Use the evaluation's report to rank upgrades by savings, and get a heat-loss calculation before buying heating equipment.
  5. Recent buyer with a CMHC-insured mortgage? Plan at least $20,000 of eligible work within the 2-year window for the 25% refund.
  6. Find a licensed service organization near you through our directory or NRCan's list (NRCan ↗).

faq.q: Are there energy efficiency rebates in Alberta in 2026?
faq.a: Not from the province, as far as we could find on October 8, 2026: the Government of Alberta's energy-efficiency programs page now returns "page not found", and the City of Edmonton says it has no residential rebates. The main help is CEIP financing in 27 municipalities, plus Lethbridge's $1,350 rebate on completed CEIP projects, Medicine Hat's HAT Smart rebates for City utility customers (up to $250 per EnerGuide evaluation; its 2026 incentive for insulation and windows is fully subscribed) and the federal CMHC Eco Improvement refund for recent buyers.

faq.q: Is there a heat pump rebate in Alberta?
faq.a: We found none. CEIP can finance an air-source heat pump in participating municipalities, Medicine Hat's HAT Smart doesn't list heat pumps, and the federal oil-to-heat-pump program that NRCan ran in Alberta closed on July 31, 2026.

faq.q: Is Calgary's Clean Energy Improvement Program open?
faq.a: Not right now. The City of Calgary says residential CEIP is closed until winter 2026/2027. When open, it finances up to 100% of costs to $50,000, at an estimated 6.00%–6.10% fixed rate, over up to 20 years.

faq.q: Does Edmonton have home energy rebates?
faq.a: No: the City says there are currently no residential rebates. Its CEIP financing is taking pre-qualifications onto a waitlist, at a 6.00% fixed rate, and residential projects need at least three upgrades.

faq.q: Do I need an EnerGuide evaluation for CEIP?
faq.a: Yes. CEIP says an EnerGuide Home Energy Evaluation is required as part of the process, and its reports estimate the savings from the upgrades you finance.

title: Saskatchewan energy efficiency rebates, grants and the Home Renovation Tax Credit (2026)
h1: Saskatchewan energy efficiency rebates, grants and the Home Renovation Tax Credit (2026)
description: What's left in Saskatchewan after the Home Efficiency Retrofit Rebate ended in April 2026: the 10.5% Home Renovation Tax Credit (up to $420 a year), SaskEnergy equipment rebates, free income-qualified upgrades and Saskatoon's HELP loans, and why we found no window grant or heat pump rebate. Checked October 8, 2026.
blurb: The rebate ended in April 2026. What's left: the 10.5% Home Renovation Tax Credit, SaskEnergy equipment rebates, free income-qualified upgrades and Saskatoon's HELP loans.
lede: Saskatchewan's Home Efficiency Retrofit Rebate ended in April 2026, and SaskEnergy's Energy Efficiency Discounts Program followed on July 27. We found no government window grant and no heat pump rebate. What remains is a 10.5% Home Renovation Tax Credit, a few utility rebates and free upgrades for income-qualified homes.

sections.html:
• Home Efficiency Retrofit Rebate: "ended in April 2026," say both SaskPower and SaskEnergy, without giving a day (SaskPower ↗, SaskEnergy ↗). The provincial page that used to describe it now returns "page not found" (saskatchewan.ca ↗).
  • SaskEnergy Energy Efficiency Discounts Program: "ended July 27, 2026" (SaskEnergy ↗).
  • Oil to Heat Pump Affordability Program: the federal program NRCan delivered directly in Saskatchewan closed to new applications on July 31, 2026 (NRCan ↗).

Neither SaskPower nor SaskEnergy lists a replacement rebate on its program pages, checked October 8, 2026.

sections.h2: The Home Renovation Tax Credit: up to $420 a year
sections.html:
The Saskatchewan Home Renovation Tax Credit is back for the 2025 and later tax years. It's a non-refundable provincial credit of 10.5% on renovation spending above a $1,000 base, on up to $5,000 of expenses: at most $420 a year, or $525 for seniors, who can claim up to $6,000 of expenses (Government of Saskatchewan ↗).

  • Who: homeowners renovating their principal residence in Saskatchewan, for expenses incurred on or after October 1, 2024. The credit can be split among family members, up to the maximum.
  • What counts: renovations of an enduring nature, such as windows and doors, a furnace, boiler or water heater, central air conditioning, permanent ventilation, electrical upgrades and solar panels, with related labour, permits and taxes.
  • What doesn't: your own labour, routine maintenance, appliances, electronics, tools and financing costs.
  • How: claim it on your personal income tax return; the Canada Revenue Agency administers it. Keep receipts or invoices showing the contractor, what was bought and when, marked "paid" or backed by proof of payment.

Worked example: $5,000 of new windows earns 10.5% of ($5,000 − $1,000) = $420 off your provincial tax. Spending more doesn't raise the credit in the same year.

sections.h2: Is there a Saskatchewan government window grant?
sections.html: We found no provincial grant for windows in 2026. The closest thing is the Home Renovation Tax Credit above: windows and doors are eligible expenses, and a $5,000 window job earns the maximum $420 credit ($525 for seniors spending $6,000). The federal Greener Homes Grant, which once paid for windows, stopped taking applications in February 2024.

SaskEnergy's Residential Equipment Replacement Rebate pays when you replace existing gas equipment with a high-efficiency model (SaskEnergy ↗):

  • Furnace (97% AFUE or better): $325
  • Boiler (95% AFUE or better, up to 300 MBH): $750; combination boiler: $800
  • Tankless water heater (0.87 UEF or better) or condensing water heater (0.80 UEF or better): $1,000

It's for replacements only, and the application must reach SaskEnergy within 120 days of installation. It doesn't cover heat pumps, insulation or windows.

SaskPower's Energy Assistance Program sends a home energy coach to install free upgrades: LED bulbs, faucet aerators, high-efficiency showerheads, a block heater timer, pipe wrap, a drying rack and, if eligible, a smart thermostat. It's for SaskPower, Saskatoon Light & Power and Swift Current Light & Power customers, owners or renters, with before-tax household income from $54,335 or less for one person up to $180,721 for ten (SaskPower ↗).

Income-qualifying homeowners who took part in that program may be eligible for a free high-efficiency furnace through SaskEnergy's Heating Affordability Program (SaskEnergy ↗).

We found no heat pump rebate in Saskatchewan: neither SaskPower nor SaskEnergy lists one for homes. In Saskatoon, the City's Home Energy Loan Program finances cold-climate air-source and ground-source heat pumps on NRCan's eligible lists. Size any heat pump from a heat-loss calculation, and compare running costs with our energy cost calculator. Other provinces are compared in heat pump rebates in Canada by province.

Saskatoon's Home Energy Loan Program is accepting applications (City of Saskatoon ↗):

  • Loans of $1,000 to $40,000, or up to $60,000 if you show the project will cut the home's energy use by 50% or more.
  • 2026 rates: 3.24% (5 years), 4.03% (10 years), 4.68% (15 years) and 4.83% (20 years), repaid through property taxes.
  • A $750 administration fee, waived with proof of low income.
  • A $1,000 rebate toward energy audits for homeowners who take part in the loan.
  • Eligible work includes insulation, air sealing, ENERGY STAR windows and doors, high-efficiency furnaces, heat pumps, HRVs and solar.

sections.h2: Planning a retrofit without a rebate
sections.html:
1. Start with an EnerGuide evaluation or at least a blower door test, so you spend on the leaks and gaps that cost the most.
  2. Do air sealing and attic insulation before replacing heating equipment, then size the new system to the improved house.
  3. Keep every receipt for the Home Renovation Tax Credit, and time large jobs across tax years if you're near the $5,000 limit.
  4. Replacing a gas furnace or water heater? Claim SaskEnergy's rebate within 120 days.
  5. Bought recently with a CMHC-insured mortgage? CMHC Eco Improvement refunds 25% of your premium after $20,000 of energy work.

faq.q: Is there a Saskatchewan government window grant?
faq.a: Not that we could find. Windows and doors are eligible expenses for the Saskatchewan Home Renovation Tax Credit instead: 10.5% of expenses above $1,000, up to $5,000, so at most $420 a year ($525 for seniors). It's non-refundable and claimed on your income tax return.

faq.q: What energy efficiency grants are available in Saskatchewan?
faq.a: As of October 8, 2026 there's no provincial energy-efficiency grant. What exists: the Home Renovation Tax Credit, SaskEnergy rebates of $325–$1,000 for replacing gas furnaces, boilers and water heaters, free upgrades through SaskPower's Energy Assistance Program for income-qualified households, and loans through Saskatoon's Home Energy Loan Program.

faq.q: Is there a heat pump rebate in Saskatchewan?
faq.a: We found none. SaskPower and SaskEnergy list no residential heat pump rebate, and the federal oil-to-heat-pump program closed on July 31, 2026. Saskatoon's Home Energy Loan Program can finance a cold-climate air-source or ground-source heat pump.

faq.q: How much is the Saskatchewan Home Renovation Tax Credit?
faq.a: 10.5% of eligible renovation expenses above $1,000, on up to $5,000 of expenses, for a maximum of $420 a year; seniors can claim up to $6,000 of expenses, for up to $525. It applies to expenses incurred on or after October 1, 2024, claimed on your 2025 or later return.

faq.q: Did the Home Efficiency Retrofit Rebate end?
faq.a: Yes. SaskPower and SaskEnergy both say it ended in April 2026, and no replacement rebate appears on their program pages.
